t.en: In Example “Verifying the inverse of a matrix”, we verified that a matrix $A$ had an inverse. But we did not actually compute the inverse: the inverse $B$ was already given, and we merely checked that $AB=I$ and $BA=I$. We now explore a method for finding the inverse when it is not already known what it is.

title.en: Finding the inverse of a matrix

t.en: Suppose $A$ is an $n\times n$-matrix. To find $A^{-1}$ if it exists, form the augmented $n\times 2n$-matrix
If possible, do row operations until you obtain an $n\times 2n$-matrix of the form
If this can be done, then $A$ is invertible and $A^{-1}=B$. If it is not possible (i.e., if the reduced echelon form of $A$ has less than $n$ pivot entries), then $A$ is not invertible.
This algorithm shows how to find the inverse if it exists. It also tells us if $A$ does not have an inverse.

title.en: Finding the inverse of a matrix

t.en: Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & 2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 3 & 1 & -1 \end{array}\right]$. Find $A^{-1}$ if it exists.
We set up the augmented matrix and reduce it to reduced echelon form.

blocks.tex:
\begin{array}{rcl}\mat{A\mid I} &=&
    \left[\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
      1 & 2 &  2 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\
      1 & 0 &  2 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\
      3 & 1 & -1 & 0 & 0 & 1
    \end{array}\right]\\[1ex]
    &\stackrel{R_2\rowop R_2-R_1}{\stackrel{R_3\rowop R_3-3R_1}{\roweq}}&
    \left[\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
      1 &  2 &  2 &  1 & 0 & 0 \\
      0 & -2 &  0 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\
      0 & -5 & -7 & -3 & 0 & 1
    \end{array}\right]\\[1ex]
    &\stackrel{R_1\rowop 7R_1}{\stackrel{R_3\rowop -2R_3}{\roweq}}&
    \left[\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
      7 & 14 & 14 &  7 & 0 &  0 \\
      0 & -2 &  0 & -1 & 1 &  0 \\
      0 & 10 & 14 &  6 & 0 & -2
    \end{array}\right]\\[1ex]
    &\stackrel{R_1\rowop R_1+7R_2}{\stackrel{R_3\rowop R_3+5R_2}{\roweq}}&
    \left[\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
      7 &  0 & 14 &  0 & 7 &  0 \\
      0 & -2 &  0 & -1 & 1 &  0 \\
      0 &  0 & 14 &  1 & 5 & -2
    \end{array}\right]\\[1ex]
    &\stackrel{R_1\rowop R_1-R_3}{\roweq}&
    \left[\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
      7 &  0 &  0 & -1 & 2 &  2 \\
      0 & -2 &  0 & -1 & 1 &  0 \\
      0 &  0 & 14 &  1 & 5 & -2
    \end{array}\right]\\[-1ex]
    &\stackrel{R_1\rowop \frac{1}{7}R_1}{\stackrel{R_2\rowop -\frac{1}{2}R_2}{\stackrel{R_3\rowop \frac{1}{14}R_3}{\roweq}}}&
    \def\arraystretch{1.5}
    \left[\begin{array}{rrr|rrr}
      1 & 0 & 0 & -\frac{1}{7} & \frac{2}{7} & \frac{2}{7} \\
      0 & 1 & 0 & \frac{1}{2} & -\frac{1}{2} & 0           \\
      0 & 0 & 1 & \frac{1}{14} & \frac{5}{14} & -\frac{1}{7}
    \end{array}\right].\end{array}

t.en: Notice that the last augmented matrix is of the form $\mat{I\mid B}$, where the left-hand side is the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix. Therefore, the inverse is the $3 \times 3$-matrix on the right-hand side, given by
When looking for the inverse of a matrix, it can happen that the left-hand side cannot be row reduced to the identity matrix. The following is an example of this situation.
Let $A=\left[\begin{array}{rrr} 1 & -2 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 & 4 \end{array}\right]$. Find $A^{-1}$ if it exists.
We write the augmented matrix
and proceed to do row operations attempting to obtain $\mat{I\mid A^{-1}}$. After a few row operations, we have

At this point, we see that the coefficient matrix has rank $2$, i.e., there are only two pivot entries. This means there is no way to obtain $I$ on the left-hand side of this augmented matrix. Hence, there is no way to complete the algorithm, and the inverse of $A$ does not exist.

If the algorithm provides an inverse, it is always possible to double-check that your answer is correct. To do so, use the method demonstrated in Example “Verifying the inverse of a matrix”. Check that the products $AA^{-1}$ and $A^{-1}A$ both equal the identity matrix. Through this method, you can always ensure that you have calculated $A^{-1}$ properly.
